title: Gradient rollouts: operational flow and gating playbook (working)
body:
Purpose and quick summary:

This is a working playbook for a "gradient rollout" pattern we want to pilot for LLM-powered features. The core idea: instead of a single binary canary (on/off) or fixed percent A/B, perform controlled, multi-axis gradual exposure across traffic percent, model fidelity (quantization / size), and latency/cost tiers. The goal is to reduce blast radius while extracting actionable signal on quality, latency, and unit economics simultaneously.

Why gradient rollouts? (short)
- Many regressions only show up when both traffic and batch patterns change; a single-dimension canary misses interactions.
- For inference, cost/latency tradeoffs are as important as quality. We need to test configurations that vary both model variant and traffic.
- Allows us to use small, fast experiments to surface problems before committing expensive capacity.

Key concepts / definitions (working):
- Cohort: a traffic slice by attribute (region, tenant tier, device, session length).
- Gradient axis: a parameter we move monotonically (examples: traffic %, model quantization level, batching aggressiveness, KV cache TTL).
- Exposure vector: an ordered list of (cohort, axis, start, target, step, schedule).
- Risk budget: a numeric budget (e.g., allowed p99 increase, allowed cost delta, allowed hallucination rate) that consumption gates progression.

High-level flow (ops timeline):
1) Pre-flight (T-72h):
   - Product owner fills short hypothesis canvas: what do we expect to change (latency, cost, quality)? win metric and guardrail metrics.
   - Engineers create a rollout YAML in the console (exposure vector + progression policy). Attach test prompt set and synthetic workload.
   - SRE / infra review for capacity and fallback. Confirm canary bucket routing rules exist.
   - QA runs smoke on staging with curated prompts and cold-start scenarios.

2) Alpha (T0 - first 2 hours):
   - Start with tiny cohort (0.1% global traffic or 1% of non-critical tenants). Model variant at lowest-risk setting (e.g., same-size model but lower quantization).
   - Collect detailed telemetry: p50/p95/p99 latency, token counts, GPU utilization, error rates, hallucination/QA score on eval set.
   - Short automated sanity checks every 5 minutes; human on-call for first hour.

3) Gradient progression (multi-step):
   - Each step: increase one axis by defined delta (e.g., traffic 0.1% -> 0.5% -> 2%), wait for stabilization window (15-60m depending on traffic), evaluate gating conditions.
   - Only progress if all gates pass. If any gate trips, either pause, step back, or trigger full rollback depending on severity.

4) Beta -> Ramp (multi-day):
   - After successful small steps, increase to broader cohorts (non-CHI regions, or paid-tier only) and/or bump model fidelity to target config.
   - Run A/B buckets in parallel for a subset of cohorts for quality regressions that need comparative analysis.

Gating rules (example thresholds — adapt per feature):
- Latency: p99 must not increase > 15% vs baseline for two consecutive windows (30m), and GPU queue depth < configured threshold.
- Errors: client error rate (4xx/5xx) increase no more than X (0.02 absolute) and server errors must stay near zero.
- Quality: on the canary prompt set, mean eval score must not drop > 3 points; hallucination rate must not increase by > 1.5x.
- Cost: cost-per-1k-tokens should not exceed target by more than 20% for more than 2 consecutive windows.
- User-impact signals (support tickets/escalations): any high-sev report relevant to the change pauses rollout.

Statistical notes for A/B comparisons:
- Use Bayesian sequential testing for small incremental traffic increases — avoids repeated-peeking bias.
- For quality metrics with high variance, run head-to-head A/B for at least N requests where N computed from baseline variance (we include a helper script in the repo).
- Flagging: if a metric trend is borderline, surface raw examples for quick QA review (link to sample log queries).

Roles & responsibilities (cross-functional):
- Product (owner): hypothesis, prompts, final go/no-go.
- Eng (owner): rollout YAML, canary hooks, metrics, fallback config.
- SRE: capacity signoff, monitoring dashboards, escalation path.
- Applied ML / Evaluation: design eval prompt set and interpret quality regressions.
- CS/Support: monitor customer signals, triage tickets.
- Legal/Security (if applicable): confirm auditing is enabled for private deploys.

Operational primitives we rely on (console features):
- Canary routing by cohort attribute and percent.
- Rollout manifests with multi-axis steps and explicit rollback policies.
- Automated gating engine (plugs into metrics cluster and alerting).
- Snapshot eval runner that scores inference outputs on a curated test set each step.
- Cost-estimator that projects incremental monthly cost at a given exposure.

Runbook (short checklist for an engineer starting a gradient rollout):
- [ ] Create hypothesis canvas + set primary/guardrail metrics.
- [ ] Register eval prompt set and link to rollout.
- [ ] Create rollout manifest (start->target, step sizes, stabilization windows).
- [ ] Run smoke tests on staging and copy routing rules to prod sandbox.
- [ ] SRE signoff (capacity + fallback path).
- [ ] Schedule rollout window and on-call coverage.
- [ ] Kick off alpha, monitor first stabilization window.
- [ ] Iterate steps; record each decision in rollout timeline.

Rollback decision logic (quick):
- Severity level 1 (soft): minor metric drift within guardrails but concerning trend -> pause, add more monitoring, escalate to ML and product for deeper review.
- Level 2 (medium): guardrail threshold crossed but limited scope -> step back to previous stable step and hold; open incident ticket.
- Level 3 (hard): critical error (large p99 spike, production error surge, major quality regression) -> immediate full rollback to last known-good variant and page SRE + Eng.

Communication templates (short):
- Pre-rollout: "Starting gradient rollout for <feature> at <time>. Alpha cohort = <cohort>. SLOs and guardrails linked: <link>. On-call: <name>."
- Pause/step-back: "Paused rollout at step X due to <metric>. Rolling back to previous step. Investigating; ETA unknown."
- Full rollback: "Full rollback executed for <feature>. Affected cohorts: <list>. Incident created: <link>. Postmortem owners: <names>."

Observability & dashboards (must-haves):
- Per-cohort latency heatmap (p50/p95/p99) with baseline overlays.
- Quality signal panel (eval set score, hallucination rate, excerpted model responses for failed prompts).
- Cost panel (tokens per request, cost per 1k tokens, GPU utilization).
- Incident & ticket correlation view (show support tickets mapped to cohort/time windows).

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- How aggressively should we tie rollback to customer-visible tickets vs metric-only signals? (ask CS)
- Should some cohorts be immune to automatic rollback (enterprise paid customers) and instead go to manual gating?
- Add a lightweight simulation tool to estimate probability of hitting guardrails given historical traffic patterns. (Ravi to prototype)
- Flesh out the Bayesian priors for the sequential test helper.

Appendix: example rollout manifest (sketch)
- name: gradient-quiet-launch
  axes:
    - name: traffic_percent
      start: 0.1
      steps: [0.5, 2, 5, 20]
    - name: model_quant
      start: q4
      steps: [q4, q8, baseline]
  cohorts: [region:EU, tier:free-nonauth]
  gates: [latency_p99:15pct, eval_drop:3points, cost_delta:20pct]
  stabilization_window: 30m

Final note: this is intentionally pragmatic and opinionated. The aim is to produce an operational pattern that scales risk-sensibly for LLM features where capacity, token cost, and quality are tightly coupled. Next steps: trial this pattern on one upcoming feature (TBD) and capture lessons in a post-run template.

Unresolved: pick default stabilization windows per traffic class (mobile vs web vs API).
